title: America’s Surprising Energy Advantage
gist: Aldy and co-authors argue China has already won the intermittent-power race — solar, wind, batteries, critical minerals — but the United States holds a durable lead in clean firm power: enhanced geothermal, where shale drilling capital and labor transfer directly, and small modular reactors, where US firms hold nearly a third of publicly available designs. The investable thesis is that AI data-center demand makes weather-independent generation more valuable than intermittent capacity, and that US export success depends on procurement consortia, 123-agreement reform, and partnership with hyperscalers rather than on subsidy-matching China.

themes.theme: AI Demand Shock Rewrites the Transition

insights.claim: Global electricity needs are expected to increase by three-quarters over the next 25 years, driven by developing-world electrification, EV adoption, and data-center proliferation.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: A 75 percent load growth baseline over 25 years underwrites structural long positions in generation, grid equipment, and transmission regardless of climate policy direction.
insights.quote: The world’s electricity needs are expected to increase by three-quarters over the next 25 years
insights.locator: Global demand for energy is surging

insights.claim: Clean energy has shifted from being a climate imperative to being the key input for economic growth and technological advancement, which decouples clean-power demand from climate politics.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Clean-power demand is now insulated from anti-climate policy swings — the AI growth motive, not decarbonization pledges, is the demand driver to model.
insights.locator: This demand shock has shifted the impetus

insights.claim: Ambitious net-zero pledges made over the past decade have fallen glaringly short of their goals even as AI-driven power demand exploded, meaning the transition is now supply-constrained rather than ambition-constrained.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Do not forecast clean-energy buildout off policy targets; forecast it off data-center load growth and equipment supply chains.
insights.locator: The clean energy transition has entered a new phase

insights.claim: Hyperscalers have hard-committed to clean sourcing, with Google promising 100 percent clean power for its data centers by 2030 and Meta matching its data centers' electricity use with renewables.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Corporate PPA demand from a handful of buyers sets the marginal price for firm clean power — track hyperscaler procurement announcements as the leading indicator for SMR and geothermal offtake.
insights.locator: Large tech companies have committed to sourcing clean power

themes.theme: China's Intermittent-Power Lock and Mineral Leverage

insights.claim: Chinese companies exported $28 billion worth of solar panels in 2024, and Chinese firms dominate global wind turbines and the battery market.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Sizes the incumbent position US policy is trying to displace — competing head-on in modules or cells is capital destruction absent extraordinary subsidy.
insights.locator: In 2024, for instance, Chinese companies exported

insights.claim: JinkoSolar has created more than 20 overseas subsidiaries, extending Chinese control over clean energy infrastructure across the developing world.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Chinese solar distribution is embedded locally, not just exported — displacing it in emerging markets requires financing and permitting help, not tariffs.
insights.locator: One of China’s largest solar companies, JinkoSolar

insights.claim: Chinese officials forced the Trump administration to lift US tariffs on Chinese products by threatening to cut the United States off from critical minerals.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Critical-mineral chokepoints have demonstrated escalation dominance over US trade policy — a proven, repeatable lever that caps how hard Washington can push on tariffs.
insights.locator: In fact, Chinese officials forced the Trump administration

insights.claim: China built its clean-tech dominance over two decades through import-tax exemptions on clean energy inputs, domestic-content sourcing requirements, and state funding for manufacturer R&D and commercialization.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The playbook is replicable but slow — any US attempt to copy it in solar arrives two decades late, which is why the authors pivot to firm power instead.
insights.locator: For more than two decades, China has lavishly supported

insights.claim: China is well positioned to become the world's new energy superpower on the strength of intermittent power and batteries alone.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Baseline scenario absent a US firm-power push: Chinese pricing power over global electricity capex, with attendant geopolitical dependency risk for buyers.
insights.quote: China is well positioned to be the world’s new energy superpower.
insights.locator: China dominates the supply of intermittent power

insights.claim: US oil and gas leverage over global energy markets is fading because most remaining hydrocarbon wealth sits under state-controlled reserves that US firms cannot access.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Resource-access limits, not demand, cap the growth ceiling of US independent E&Ps' international expansion.
insights.locator: But such leverage is fading as the fossil fuel industry

insights.claim: Alternative energy sources are becoming cheaper than fossil fuels and are less vulnerable to blockades like the one now choking off the Strait of Hormuz, accelerating buyer diversification away from hydrocarbons.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Each Hormuz disruption permanently pulls forward clean-power demand rather than only spiking oil — the supply-security premium now accrues to non-fossil generation.
insights.locator: Countries and corporations are also looking into alternative sources

insights.claim: The Philippines and Saudi Arabia have both made clean energy central to their national development strategies, including a major oil exporter positioning away from its own product.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Petrostate clean-energy pivots signal where the export market for US firm-power technology actually is — Gulf capital is a buyer, not a competitor.
insights.locator: The Philippines and Saudi Arabia, for instance

insights.claim: The Trump administration's strategy of expanding coal, gas, and oil output through federal-land access and LNG deals with Asian and European partners is unlikely to succeed on its own, because future electricity systems will lean on renewables and nuclear.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: US federal energy policy is misaligned with the growth segment — the export upside is in firm clean technology, not in incremental barrels or cargoes.
insights.locator: Alternatively, Washington could triple its commitment to fossil fuels

insights.claim: Directly matching China in solar panels and EVs — the Biden administration's 2022 Inflation Reduction Act approach — cannot work because Chinese price points are unbeatable absent extraordinary US subsidies.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Bearish on subsidy-dependent US module and cell manufacturers; the durable US positions are in technologies where China lacks a cost head start.
insights.locator: The first is to compete with China directly

insights.claim: Enhanced geothermal is now viable across most of the world because new techniques create reservoirs or reach the required heat far closer to the surface, ending the constraint that limited sites to the 25,000-mile Ring of Fire.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The addressable market for geothermal expanded from a handful of volcanic geographies to nearly global — a step-change in total addressable market for drilling services.
insights.locator: Once, geothermal deployment depended on natural geological formations

insights.claim: Geothermal drilling costs have been nearly halved since the early 2020s and continue to fall in the United States thanks to the Department of Energy's FORGE field laboratory in Utah.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: A ~50 percent cost decline in under five years is the classic learning-curve inflection that precedes commercial scaling — watch FORGE data releases for the next leg.
insights.locator: Drilling remains expensive, but the costs have been nearly halved

insights.claim: Decades of US shale innovation created physical capital, supply chains, and labor skills that transfer directly to geothermal: oil rigs, wells, and fracking equipment can be repurposed, and oil and gas workers already have subsurface drilling and borehole expertise.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Oilfield service companies and rig owners are the unpriced call option on geothermal — the same asset base serves both, offsetting drilling overhead.
insights.locator: Decades of U.S. innovation in the oil and gas sector

insights.claim: Geothermal deployment is deterred by high upfront drilling costs, uncertainty over whether a project will actually yield a reservoir, and seven-to-ten-year deployment timelines.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Subsurface risk is the binding constraint on private capital — the sector needs resource insurance or public risk-sharing before it clears normal hurdle rates.
insights.locator: Novel geothermal systems face a similar challenge

insights.claim: The International Geothermal Commission for Standards is chaired by a Chinese oil and gas company, giving Beijing agenda-setting power over the technical rules of a sector where America leads.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Standards capture is a quiet competitive channel — Chinese-chaired standards bodies can raise compliance costs for US geothermal exporters before any market exists.
insights.locator: Washington might also consider creating an alternative forum

themes.theme: Nuclear Scoreboard and the SMR Bet

insights.claim: The United States has 94 operational nuclear plants but none under construction, while China operates 60 reactors with 37 under construction and Russia has 34 in operation with five under construction.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The construction pipeline — 37 versus zero — is the metric that determines who owns the nuclear supply chain in a decade, and it is currently a rout.
insights.locator: The United States has 94 operational nuclear plants

insights.claim: China has halved the construction cost of traditional nuclear plants over ten years, while a traditional US reactor still takes over a decade and more than $10 billion to build.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The cost gap makes conventional large-reactor exports uncompetitive for US vendors — the entire US nuclear export case rests on modularity.
insights.locator: In ten years, China has been able to halve the construction costs

insights.claim: Small modular reactors generate up to 350 megawatts per unit — about a third of a traditional reactor's capacity — but standardized designs and lower upfront cost make them saleable to customers unwilling to fund nuclear megaprojects.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: SMR economics are a bet on serial-production learning curves rather than scale economics — the unit-cost trajectory across the first dozen units is the number to track.
insights.locator: They generate up to 350 megawatts of power per unit

insights.claim: American companies account for nearly a third of publicly available small modular reactor designs, more than China and Russia combined, backed by well-funded startups including Kairos Power, TerraPower, and X-energy.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The named private SMR cohort is the direct equity expression of the US firm-power thesis; design diversity is the specific US advantage over state-directed rivals.
insights.locator: And right now, American companies account for nearly a third

insights.claim: Beijing and Moscow treat nuclear power as a geostrategic instrument and subsidize deployment through below-market loans, state credits, and subsidies, competing on financing rather than technology.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: US vendors lose deals on export financing terms, not engineering — DFC and Ex-Im style credit is the decisive competitive variable.
insights.locator: Beijing and Moscow both view nuclear power

insights.claim: SMR manufacturers must still prove to investors that per-unit costs can fall enough to offset their lower relative power output, which is the unresolved commercial risk in the technology.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The bear case on SMRs is unit economics, not safety or permitting — demand order books without demonstrated cost declines before underwriting the sector.
insights.locator: Although small modular reactors are much cheaper

insights.claim: The United States imports 99 percent of its uranium, only six countries handle the vast majority of global enrichment, and nearly half of that enrichment takes place in Russia.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Russian enrichment dependence is the single largest structural risk to a US nuclear scale-up — domestic and allied enrichment capacity is the bottleneck asset to own.
insights.locator: Right now, the United States imports 99 percent of its uranium

insights.claim: A small set of firms in China, Japan, and Russia manufacture the components used to build nuclear reactors, concentrating the reactor supply chain outside US control.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Heavy forging and reactor-component capacity is a bottleneck that will constrain any nuclear buildout schedule regardless of order volumes.
insights.locator: A small set of firms in China, Japan, and Russia

insights.claim: The Sapporo 5 partnership commits Canada, France, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States to spend $4 billion on uranium sourcing and enrichment to reduce Russian influence over nuclear fuel supply chains.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: A $4 billion allied fuel-cycle program is the concrete capital flow into Western enrichment and conversion — a near-term revenue pool for non-Russian fuel suppliers.
insights.locator: The Sapporo 5 partnership—in which Canada, France

insights.claim: US nuclear exports require bilateral 123 agreements that take 400 days on average to negotiate, and precise licensing pathways for small modular reactors remain undeveloped and country specific.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: A 400-day regulatory lead time per country is the real gating factor on SMR export revenue — standardized 123 packages would be the catalyst that unlocks the pipeline.
insights.locator: These agreements, known as 123 agreements

insights.claim: International geothermal deployment requires approvals from multiple central-government, environmental, and water regulators, producing disjointed rules and lengthy, uncertain permitting.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Multi-regulator permitting is the hidden cost line in geothermal project models — harmonized standards would compress timelines and re-rate developers.
insights.locator: International geothermal deployment often requires approvals

insights.claim: Long-term allied government procurement commitments for small modular reactors, structured with tiered pricing that charges more for early units and less for later ones, would de-risk both manufacturers and customers while cutting US reliance on Russian enriched uranium.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Tiered advance-market commitments are the specific mechanism to watch; their appearance in allied budgets would validate SMR order books.
insights.locator: The United States should secure long-term procurement commitments

insights.claim: Amazon, Google, and Meta have all begun entering long-term agreements with small modular reactor manufacturers, making hyperscalers the anchor demand for US nuclear technology.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler balance sheets substitute for utility ratebase in financing first-of-a-kind nuclear — a structural change in how new generation gets funded.
insights.locator: These efforts could also engage major corporations

insights.claim: A buyers' consortium of utilities, tech firms, and interested countries would aggregate demand for nuclear and geothermal, letting operators drive costs down through repeated exports and extending US influence abroad.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Demand aggregation is the policy lever that converts a technology lead into a cost lead — a template applicable to any first-of-a-kind energy technology.
insights.locator: The United States should also set up a buyers’ consortium

insights.claim: American tech giants building billion-dollar data centers globally contributed to more than a fifth of global greenfield foreign investment in 2025, giving them direct influence over foreign energy markets.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex is now a macro-scale FDI channel — host-country power policy will increasingly be shaped by data-center siting negotiations.
insights.locator: A handful of American tech giants are building billion-dollar data centers

insights.claim: The Stargate Project, a 2025 joint venture among American, Emirati, and Japanese firms planning $500 billion of AI infrastructure over four years, has OpenAI negotiating data-center and energy agreements directly with foreign governments.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: A private AI company conducting de facto energy diplomacy is the new dealmaking template — future bundles could package US reactors and geothermal into data-center deals.
insights.locator: A potential model to follow would be the Stargate Project

insights.claim: Stargate's first international agreement pairs a large Abu Dhabi data-center campus powered by local nuclear and solar with equally large reciprocal Emirati investment in US data centers.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: Reciprocal-capacity deals are how sovereign AI ambitions get financed — expect more Gulf-for-US data-center swaps tied to local nuclear buildout.
insights.locator: The first international agreement to come out of Stargate

insights.claim: Clean, firm power that runs around the clock is more valuable than intermittent solar and wind for powering the AI boom, which is why the geothermal-plus-nuclear position could outrank China's manufacturing lead.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Aldy
insights.so_what: The core trade: overweight firm clean generation relative to intermittent capacity, because data-center load factors reward availability over levelized cost.
insights.quote: Clean power is what governments and corporations want.
insights.locator: There is a more promising option for the United States
